prompt: Leo has just finished a long run on a hot afternoon. Put his moments in the order drive theory describes.

steps.text: After the run, Leo's body is short of water.
steps.explanation: It starts with an unmet need.

steps.text: A dry mouth and a pounding head leave him feeling uncomfortable.
steps.explanation: The unmet need creates an uncomfortable internal state called a drive.

steps.text: He heads straight into the corner shop and grabs a cold bottle of water.
steps.explanation: The drive pushes the consumer toward an action that reduces the discomfort.

steps.text: He drinks the whole bottle on the bench outside.
The discomfort fades, and Leo feels like himself again.
steps.explanation: After the need is satisfied, tension falls and the consumer returns to a more balanced state.

prompt: Each case turns on one belief from expectancy theory. Which belief is it about?

cases.text: Nadia doubts she could follow the meal-kit recipes well enough to cook a good dinner.
cases.explanation: Expectancy is the belief that effort will lead to good performance. Nadia doubts her effort would lead to a good dinner.

cases.text: Tom is sure he can finish the online coding course, but he doubts the certificate will get him hired.
cases.explanation: Instrumentality is the belief that good performance will lead to a desired outcome. Tom doubts that finishing (performance) leads to a job (outcome).

cases.text: Aisha knows the training plan would make her 5K faster, but she doesn't much care about her time.
cases.explanation: Valence is the value the consumer places on the outcome. A faster time is worth little to Aisha.

cases.text: A language app's ad shows that ten minutes a day is enough to pass the exam.
cases.explanation: The ad makes the goal seem possible: a small effort leads to good performance. That is expectancy.

cases.text: A camera brand shows customers' sharp photos winning contests and getting published.
cases.explanation: Good photos (performance) lead to prizes and publication (a desired outcome). That link is instrumentality.

cases.text: A skincare ad reminds buyers how good it feels when friends compliment their skin.
cases.explanation: The ad raises the value placed on the outcome, so the result feels valuable. That is valence.

prompt: Sort each case: is it a need, a want, or demand?

cards.text: Staying warm on a freezing winter morning
cards.explanation: A basic biological requirement, like hunger or safety.

cards.text: Feeling accepted by a new group of classmates
cards.explanation: Belonging is a basic psychological requirement.

cards.text: Picking sushi as the way to deal with lunchtime hunger
cards.explanation: Sushi is the specific product chosen to satisfy the need (hunger).

cards.text: Dreaming of a particular sports car with no way to pay for it
cards.explanation: A specific product, but without the ability to pay it is a want, not demand.

cards.text: Having the money, and being ready to pay it, for one pair of noise-cancelling headphones
cards.explanation: A want supported by both the ability and willingness to pay.

cards.text: A traveller with savings who books one particular hotel for tonight
cards.explanation: The want is backed by the ability to pay and the willingness to do it.

prompt: Match each level of Maslow's hierarchy with the purchase that serves it.

pairs.match: A blackout eye mask so a night-shift nurse can sleep during the day.
pairs.explanation: Physiological needs include food, water, and sleep.

pairs.match: A smoke alarm and a stronger door lock for a first apartment.
pairs.explanation: Safety needs include protection, stability, and health.

pairs.match: A club jersey so a new member fits in with the rest of the team.
pairs.explanation: Belonging and esteem needs include friendship, acceptance, achievement, and status.

pairs.match: Pottery lessons for someone who has always wanted to become a potter.
pairs.explanation: Self-actualization involves growth and becoming the person one wants to be.

prompt: Each shopper below faces a difficult choice. Name the motivational conflict in each case.

cases.text: Mia has saved enough for either a concert ticket or new running shoes. She wants both, but she can only buy one.
cases.explanation: Approach-approach conflict: two attractive options, but only one can be chosen.

cases.text: Lena's car has broken down. She can pay for an expensive repair, or take a long, crowded bus to work every day.
cases.explanation: Avoidance-avoidance conflict: every available option has an unwanted consequence.

cases.text: Omar wants the rich chocolate cake for the weekend, but he dreads all the calories that come with it.
cases.explanation: Approach-avoidance conflict: the same option has an attractive benefit and an unpleasant cost.

cases.text: Jonah has been offered two sunny apartments near campus. He loves both, but he can rent only one.
cases.explanation: Approach-approach conflict: two attractive options, but only one can be chosen.

cases.text: A new game console would be great fun for Sam, but buying it would use up most of his savings.
cases.explanation: Approach-avoidance conflict: the same option has an attractive benefit and an unpleasant cost.

cases.text: Priya can sit through an unpleasant dentist visit now, or risk a painful toothache later.
cases.explanation: Avoidance-avoidance conflict: every available option has an unwanted consequence.

prompt: Each shopper explains a choice. Sort the reasons by the value behind them.

cards.text: “I bought this laptop because the battery lasts all day and it never crashes.”
“I switched banks because paying with one tap on my phone is easier.”
“I wear the club scarf so everyone at the match knows I'm one of them.”
cards.explanation: Belonging and how others see the consumer: social values.

cards.text: “People at work notice this watch. It says I've made it.”
“We bought the theme-park passes just for the thrill of the rides.”
“I chose the soft wool blanket because curling up in it feels so cosy.”
